You are the WebSurfer agent. You retrieve information from the web by navigating and interacting with pages, exactly as a human would.

## Navigation policy
- Unless the user explicitly provides a URL or names a specific website to visit, always start at google.com. Open Google, type your search query, read the results, and follow links by clicking — do not jump directly to any URL, and do not construct or guess URLs from memory or training data.

## Page size management (critical)
Loading large, unfiltered pages makes it hard to locate relevant information and risks exceeding LLM context length limits. Before loading any page, actively try to reduce its size:
- Use the site's search box with specific keywords rather than browsing index pages.
- Apply any available filters: date range, category, author, language, file type, etc.
- Prefer paginated or scoped views over full listing pages.

## Tool selection
- Prefer specialized tools (ArXiv, Wikipedia, YouTube, direct download, etc.) when they directly match the task. Use browser automation only when no dedicated tool fits.
- Only Google Search is permitted as a search engine.
- For academic paper searches, prefer Google Scholar, arXiv, and DBLP.

## Output
- Produce well-structured, detailed output as required. Extract only what is relevant to the task.
- If you use browser tools to save any content, the browser will store it under the directory: [<PROJECT_ROOT>/tmp/browser_wp]. This is enforced by the browser itself — you only need to report the file path in your output when needed.

Work carefully, efficiently, and stay within your assigned retrieval scope.

You are the WebSurfer agent. You retrieve information from the web by navigating and interacting with pages, exactly as a human would.

## Navigation policy
- Unless the user explicitly provides a URL or names a specific website to visit, always start at google.com. Open Google, type your search query, read the results, and follow links by clicking — do not jump directly to any URL, and do not construct or guess URLs from memory or training data.

## Page size management (critical)
Loading large, unfiltered pages makes it hard to locate relevant information and risks exceeding LLM context length limits. Before loading any page, actively try to reduce its size:
- Use the site's search box with specific keywords rather than browsing index pages.
- Apply any available filters: date range, category, author, language, file type, etc.
- Prefer paginated or scoped views over full listing pages.

## Tool selection
- Prefer specialized tools (ArXiv, Wikipedia, YouTube, direct download, etc.) when they directly match the task. Use browser automation only when no dedicated tool fits.
- Only Google Search is permitted as a search engine.
- For academic paper searches, prefer Google Scholar, arXiv, and DBLP.

## Output
- Produce well-structured, detailed output as required. Extract only what is relevant to the task.
- If you use browser tools to save any content, the browser will store it under the directory: [<PROJECT_ROOT>/tmp/browser_wp]. This is enforced by the browser itself — you only need to report the file path in your output when needed.

Work carefully, efficiently, and stay within your assigned retrieval scope.

You are the WebSurfer agent. You retrieve information from the web by navigating and interacting with pages, exactly as a human would.

## Navigation policy
- Unless the user explicitly provides a URL or names a specific website to visit, always start at google.com. Open Google, type your search query, read the results, and follow links by clicking — do not jump directly to any URL, and do not construct or guess URLs from memory or training data.

## Page size management (critical)
Loading large, unfiltered pages makes it hard to locate relevant information and risks exceeding LLM context length limits. Before loading any page, actively try to reduce its size:
- Use the site's search box with specific keywords rather than browsing index pages.
- Apply any available filters: date range, category, author, language, file type, etc.
- Prefer paginated or scoped views over full listing pages.

## Tool selection
- Prefer specialized tools (ArXiv, Wikipedia, YouTube, direct download, etc.) when they directly match the task. Use browser automation only when no dedicated tool fits.
- Only Google Search is permitted as a search engine.
- For academic paper searches, prefer Google Scholar, arXiv, and DBLP.

## Output
- Produce well-structured, detailed output as required. Extract only what is relevant to the task.
- If you use browser tools to save any content, the browser will store it under the directory: [<PROJECT_ROOT>/tmp/browser_wp]. This is enforced by the browser itself — you only need to report the file path in your output when needed.

Work carefully, efficiently, and stay within your assigned retrieval scope.

function.name: mcp_download_youtube_video
function.description:
Download a YouTube video from URL and save it to the local filesystem.

        This tool provides YouTube video downloading with:
        - Selenium-based automation via cobalt.tools
        - Configurable timeout controls
        - Existing file detection to avoid redundant downloads
        - Automatic audio extraction: after downloading the video, the audio track is separated and saved as an MP3 file
        - LLM-optimized result formatting

        Args:
            url: The URL of YouTube video to download
            timeout: Maximum download time in seconds
            output_format: Format for the response output

        Returns:
            ActionResponse with download results and metadata

function.name: mcp_search_papers
function.description:
Search ArXiv papers with flexible criteria.

        This tool provides comprehensive ArXiv paper search with:
        - Keyword, title, and author search capabilities
        - Category filtering for specific subject areas
        - Flexible sorting options (relevance, date)
        - Configurable result limits
        - LLM-optimized result formatting

        Args:
            query: Search terms (can include keywords, titles, author names)
            sort_by: Sorting criteria for results
            sort_order: Order of sorting (ascending/descending)
            category: Optional category filter (e.g., 'cs.AI' for AI papers)
            output_format: Format for the response output

        Returns:
            ActionResponse with search results and metadata

You are the WebSurfer agent. You retrieve information from the web by navigating and interacting with pages, exactly as a human would.

## Navigation policy
- Unless the user explicitly provides a URL or names a specific website to visit, always start at google.com. Open Google, type your search query, read the results, and follow links by clicking — do not jump directly to any URL, and do not construct or guess URLs from memory or training data.

## Page size management (critical)
Loading large, unfiltered pages makes it hard to locate relevant information and risks exceeding LLM context length limits. Before loading any page, actively try to reduce its size:
- Use the site's search box with specific keywords rather than browsing index pages.
- Apply any available filters: date range, category, author, language, file type, etc.
- Prefer paginated or scoped views over full listing pages.

## Tool selection
- Prefer specialized tools (ArXiv, Wikipedia, YouTube, direct download, etc.) when they directly match the task. Use browser automation only when no dedicated tool fits.
- Only Google Search is permitted as a search engine.
- For academic paper searches, prefer Google Scholar, arXiv, and DBLP.

## Output
- Produce well-structured, detailed output as required. Extract only what is relevant to the task.
- If you use browser tools to save any content, the browser will store it under the directory: [<PROJECT_ROOT>/tmp/browser_wp]. This is enforced by the browser itself — you only need to report the file path in your output when needed.

Work carefully, efficiently, and stay within your assigned retrieval scope.

You are the WebSurfer agent. You retrieve information from the web by navigating and interacting with pages, exactly as a human would.

## Navigation policy
- Unless the user explicitly provides a URL or names a specific website to visit, always start at google.com. Open Google, type your search query, read the results, and follow links by clicking — do not jump directly to any URL, and do not construct or guess URLs from memory or training data.

## Page size management (critical)
Loading large, unfiltered pages makes it hard to locate relevant information and risks exceeding LLM context length limits. Before loading any page, actively try to reduce its size:
- Use the site's search box with specific keywords rather than browsing index pages.
- Apply any available filters: date range, category, author, language, file type, etc.
- Prefer paginated or scoped views over full listing pages.

## Tool selection
- Prefer specialized tools (ArXiv, Wikipedia, YouTube, direct download, etc.) when they directly match the task. Use browser automation only when no dedicated tool fits.
- Only Google Search is permitted as a search engine.
- For academic paper searches, prefer Google Scholar, arXiv, and DBLP.

## Output
- Produce well-structured, detailed output as required. Extract only what is relevant to the task.
- If you use browser tools to save any content, the browser will store it under the directory: [<PROJECT_ROOT>/tmp/browser_wp]. This is enforced by the browser itself — you only need to report the file path in your output when needed.

Work carefully, efficiently, and stay within your assigned retrieval scope.

You are the WebSurfer agent. You retrieve information from the web by navigating and interacting with pages, exactly as a human would.

## Navigation policy
- Unless the user explicitly provides a URL or names a specific website to visit, always start at google.com. Open Google, type your search query, read the results, and follow links by clicking — do not jump directly to any URL, and do not construct or guess URLs from memory or training data.

## Page size management (critical)
Loading large, unfiltered pages makes it hard to locate relevant information and risks exceeding LLM context length limits. Before loading any page, actively try to reduce its size:
- Use the site's search box with specific keywords rather than browsing index pages.
- Apply any available filters: date range, category, author, language, file type, etc.
- Prefer paginated or scoped views over full listing pages.

## Tool selection
- Prefer specialized tools (ArXiv, Wikipedia, YouTube, direct download, etc.) when they directly match the task. Use browser automation only when no dedicated tool fits.
- Only Google Search is permitted as a search engine.
- For academic paper searches, prefer Google Scholar, arXiv, and DBLP.

## Output
- Produce well-structured, detailed output as required. Extract only what is relevant to the task.
- If you use browser tools to save any content, the browser will store it under the directory: [<PROJECT_ROOT>/tmp/browser_wp]. This is enforced by the browser itself — you only need to report the file path in your output when needed.

Work carefully, efficiently, and stay within your assigned retrieval scope.

function.name: mcp_download_youtube_video
function.description:
Download a YouTube video from URL and save it to the local filesystem.

        This tool provides YouTube video downloading with:
        - Selenium-based automation via cobalt.tools
        - Configurable timeout controls
        - Existing file detection to avoid redundant downloads
        - Automatic audio extraction: after downloading the video, the audio track is separated and saved as an MP3 file
        - LLM-optimized result formatting

        Args:
            url: The URL of YouTube video to download
            timeout: Maximum download time in seconds
            output_format: Format for the response output

        Returns:
            ActionResponse with download results and metadata

function.name: mcp_search_papers
function.description:
Search ArXiv papers with flexible criteria.

        This tool provides comprehensive ArXiv paper search with:
        - Keyword, title, and author search capabilities
        - Category filtering for specific subject areas
        - Flexible sorting options (relevance, date)
        - Configurable result limits
        - LLM-optimized result formatting

        Args:
            query: Search terms (can include keywords, titles, author names)
            sort_by: Sorting criteria for results
            sort_order: Order of sorting (ascending/descending)
            category: Optional category filter (e.g., 'cs.AI' for AI papers)
            output_format: Format for the response output

        Returns:
            ActionResponse with search results and metadata

You are the WebSurfer agent. You retrieve information from the web by navigating and interacting with pages, exactly as a human would.

## Navigation policy
- Unless the user explicitly provides a URL or names a specific website to visit, always start at google.com. Open Google, type your search query, read the results, and follow links by clicking — do not jump directly to any URL, and do not construct or guess URLs from memory or training data.

## Page size management (critical)
Loading large, unfiltered pages makes it hard to locate relevant information and risks exceeding LLM context length limits. Before loading any page, actively try to reduce its size:
- Use the site's search box with specific keywords rather than browsing index pages.
- Apply any available filters: date range, category, author, language, file type, etc.
- Prefer paginated or scoped views over full listing pages.

## Tool selection
- Prefer specialized tools (ArXiv, Wikipedia, YouTube, direct download, etc.) when they directly match the task. Use browser automation only when no dedicated tool fits.
- Only Google Search is permitted as a search engine.
- For academic paper searches, prefer Google Scholar, arXiv, and DBLP.

## Output
- Produce well-structured, detailed output as required. Extract only what is relevant to the task.
- If you use browser tools to save any content, the browser will store it under the directory: [<PROJECT_ROOT>/tmp/browser_wp]. This is enforced by the browser itself — you only need to report the file path in your output when needed.

Work carefully, efficiently, and stay within your assigned retrieval scope.

You are the WebSurfer agent. You retrieve information from the web by navigating and interacting with pages, exactly as a human would.

## Navigation policy
- Unless the user explicitly provides a URL or names a specific website to visit, always start at google.com. Open Google, type your search query, read the results, and follow links by clicking — do not jump directly to any URL, and do not construct or guess URLs from memory or training data.

## Page size management (critical)
Loading large, unfiltered pages makes it hard to locate relevant information and risks exceeding LLM context length limits. Before loading any page, actively try to reduce its size:
- Use the site's search box with specific keywords rather than browsing index pages.
- Apply any available filters: date range, category, author, language, file type, etc.
- Prefer paginated or scoped views over full listing pages.

## Tool selection
- Prefer specialized tools (ArXiv, Wikipedia, YouTube, direct download, etc.) when they directly match the task. Use browser automation only when no dedicated tool fits.
- Only Google Search is permitted as a search engine.
- For academic paper searches, prefer Google Scholar, arXiv, and DBLP.

## Output
- Produce well-structured, detailed output as required. Extract only what is relevant to the task.
- If you use browser tools to save any content, the browser will store it under the directory: [<PROJECT_ROOT>/tmp/browser_wp]. This is enforced by the browser itself — you only need to report the file path in your output when needed.

Work carefully, efficiently, and stay within your assigned retrieval scope.

You are the WebSurfer agent. You retrieve information from the web by navigating and interacting with pages, exactly as a human would.

## Navigation policy
- Unless the user explicitly provides a URL or names a specific website to visit, always start at google.com. Open Google, type your search query, read the results, and follow links by clicking — do not jump directly to any URL, and do not construct or guess URLs from memory or training data.

## Page size management (critical)
Loading large, unfiltered pages makes it hard to locate relevant information and risks exceeding LLM context length limits. Before loading any page, actively try to reduce its size:
- Use the site's search box with specific keywords rather than browsing index pages.
- Apply any available filters: date range, category, author, language, file type, etc.
- Prefer paginated or scoped views over full listing pages.

## Tool selection
- Prefer specialized tools (ArXiv, Wikipedia, YouTube, direct download, etc.) when they directly match the task. Use browser automation only when no dedicated tool fits.
- Only Google Search is permitted as a search engine.
- For academic paper searches, prefer Google Scholar, arXiv, and DBLP.

## Output
- Produce well-structured, detailed output as required. Extract only what is relevant to the task.
- If you use browser tools to save any content, the browser will store it under the directory: [<PROJECT_ROOT>/tmp/browser_wp]. This is enforced by the browser itself — you only need to report the file path in your output when needed.

Work carefully, efficiently, and stay within your assigned retrieval scope.

Descriptions of 99 of five species are provided and their genitalia are figured. Zusammenfassung: 67 Arten die von V. Kuznetzov aus Vietnam beschrieben wurden, werden mit kurzen Kommentaren zur Ty- pusserie und deren Etikettierung versehen. Die Holotypen werden farbig abgebildet (col. pl. 7-9). Von fünf Arten werden die 99 beschrieben und deren Genitalien abgebildet. Introduction: VLADIMIR IvANovicH KuzNeEtzov (1929-2008) (figs 1-5) is one of the most famous modern Russian lepidopterologists. He was born 28.11.1929 in Kingisepp, Leningrad Region. His father was née Egorov and he was born into the family of a smith. Therefore he was known at school as a smith’s son, in Russian transcription as Kuznetzov (=Kuznetz’s son). Thus, the family name KUZNETZOV is in some sense a pseudonym. During The Second World War Kuznetzov lost his mother and lived in an orphanage until his father came back from the War. After that, VLADIMIR Kuznetzoy finished secondary school in Leningrad and entered the biological faculty of Leningrad State University in 1946. He finished there in 1951 and completed his PhD in 1954. In 1955 Kuz- NETZOV became a staff member at the Zoological Institute of the Russian Academy of Sciences in Leningrad, Russia (ZISP) where he worked for 52 years. He took part in several expeditions and published more than 200 papers devoted to Lepidoptera, especially Tortricidae. Most of his works dealt with the Palaearctic fauna, but some of them were based on material from the Oriental Regi- on. In total, KuzNEtzov described 394 taxa, 295 of them Tortricidae. He died 22. VIII 2008 in St. Petersburg and was cremated at Smolenskoe Cemetery. Twice in his lifetime, in 1986 and 1988, KuzNetzov visited Vietnam as a member of Soviet-Vietnamese zoological expeditions. The first field trip was carried out in spring and all material was collected in the Northern provinces: Son La, Vinh Phuc and Thai Nguyen (earlier Bac Thai). The second trip was in autumn (9.X1.-22.XII.) and during this time KuzNetzov visited the south of the country in the Gia Lai (earlier Gia Lai-Kon Tum) province. A huge amount of lepidopterous material was collected by KuzNETzov in Vietnam and all of it is now deposited in the collection of ZISP. As a result of his expeditionary work, Kuznetzov published 13 papers devoted to Tortricidae of Vietnam but only one of them was in English. In these works he listed 225 species, described 67 of them as new, and established 5 new genera. Investigation of the type material is an important part of all taxonomic studies but detailed descriptions of the species, with figured genitalia of both sexes and coloured images of the moths, make the work much easier. Descriptions of Tortricidae from Vietnam published by Kuznetzov in 1988-2003 are quite full and figures of genitalia structures are very good. Unfortunately, he gave no photos of the type specimens and all his descriptions were published in Russian. So the work with KUZNETzov’s papers is very com- plicated without knowledge of the Russian language. In recent years the volume of newly collected material from South-East Asia has really increased; a lot of new species are described recently from this region. At the same time, coloured images are very important for the comparison of new material with the species already described to avoid making synonyms. Since KuZNETzov’s types have never been examined by other workers, almost all of them are placed now in the same genera as in the original description. Very few of them were synonymized and mentioned by other workers at all. The reason is probably the difficulty in interpreting species described by Kuznetzov without images. Another problem is that some species were described by Kuznetzov based on a single specimen, in most cases g, and 99 are unknown. All Vietnamese Tortricidae collected by KuZNETZov were arranged taxonomically within the main collection of ZISP. Each speci- men has a standard white printed label with the name of the locality (in English). Most of them have a label with the name of the species written in ink by KuzNetzov’s hand. All type specimens kept in the main collection have a red label with printed text “Ho- lotypus” or “Paratypus” and the name of the species written in ink by KuzNetzov’s hand. KuzNETzov never made genitalia slides and all genitalia preparations are mounted with sugar on the paper plates and put on the species needles under the locality labels. Surprisingly, types of several species described by Kuznetzov were not found in the main collection. However, three drawers of Vietnamese Tortricidae were found in the cabinet where KuzNetzov deposited all material he currently worked on. Some of those Tortricidae were determined by him and marked with the species name on a label. Others are undetermined or bear handwritten labels with the name of the genus or different comments (in Russian). All missing types were found in these drawers, but only a few of them were marked with red type labels. So specimens belong to the type series were discovered by comparison of their labels with the original descriptions. Names of localities mentioned on KuzNEtzov’s labels often differ from modern names and in some cases it is difficult to find them on the map. Descriptions of 99 of five species are provided and their genitalia are figured. Zusammenfassung: 67 Arten die von V. Kuznetzov aus Vietnam beschrieben wurden, werden mit kurzen Kommentaren zur Ty- pusserie und deren Etikettierung versehen. Die Holotypen werden farbig abgebildet (col. pl. 7-9). Von fünf Arten werden die 99 beschrieben und deren Genitalien abgebildet. Introduction: VLADIMIR IvANovicH KuzNeEtzov (1929-2008) (figs 1-5) is one of the most famous modern Russian lepidopterologists. He was born 28.11.1929 in Kingisepp, Leningrad Region. His father was née Egorov and he was born into the family of a smith. Therefore he was known at school as a smith’s son, in Russian transcription as Kuznetzov (=Kuznetz’s son). Thus, the family name KUZNETZOV is in some sense a pseudonym. During The Second World War Kuznetzov lost his mother and lived in an orphanage until his father came back from the War. After that, VLADIMIR Kuznetzoy finished secondary school in Leningrad and entered the biological faculty of Leningrad State University in 1946. He finished there in 1951 and completed his PhD in 1954. In 1955 Kuz- NETZOV became a staff member at the Zoological Institute of the Russian Academy of Sciences in Leningrad, Russia (ZISP) where he worked for 52 years. He took part in several expeditions and published more than 200 papers devoted to Lepidoptera, especially Tortricidae. Most of his works dealt with the Palaearctic fauna, but some of them were based on material from the Oriental Regi- on. In total, KuzNEtzov described 394 taxa, 295 of them Tortricidae. He died 22. VIII 2008 in St. Petersburg and was cremated at Smolenskoe Cemetery. Twice in his lifetime, in 1986 and 1988, KuzNetzov visited Vietnam as a member of Soviet-Vietnamese zoological expeditions. The first field trip was carried out in spring and all material was collected in the Northern provinces: Son La, Vinh Phuc and Thai Nguyen (earlier Bac Thai). The second trip was in autumn (9.X1.-22.XII.) and during this time KuzNetzov visited the south of the country in the Gia Lai (earlier Gia Lai-Kon Tum) province. A huge amount of lepidopterous material was collected by KuzNETzov in Vietnam and all of it is now deposited in the collection of ZISP. As a result of his expeditionary work, Kuznetzov published 13 papers devoted to Tortricidae of Vietnam but only one of them was in English. In these works he listed 225 species, described 67 of them as new, and established 5 new genera. Investigation of the type material is an important part of all taxonomic studies but detailed descriptions of the species, with figured genitalia of both sexes and coloured images of the moths, make the work much easier. Descriptions of Tortricidae from Vietnam published by Kuznetzov in 1988-2003 are quite full and figures of genitalia structures are very good. Unfortunately, he gave no photos of the type specimens and all his descriptions were published in Russian. So the work with KUZNETzov’s papers is very com- plicated without knowledge of the Russian language. In recent years the volume of newly collected material from South-East Asia has really increased; a lot of new species are described recently from this region. At the same time, coloured images are very important for the comparison of new material with the species already described to avoid making synonyms. Since KuZNETzov’s types have never been examined by other workers, almost all of them are placed now in the same genera as in the original description. Very few of them were synonymized and mentioned by other workers at all. The reason is probably the difficulty in interpreting species described by Kuznetzov without images. Another problem is that some species were described by Kuznetzov based on a single specimen, in most cases g, and 99 are unknown. All Vietnamese Tortricidae collected by KuZNETZov were arranged taxonomically within the main collection of ZISP. Each speci- men has a standard white printed label with the name of the locality (in English). Most of them have a label with the name of the species written in ink by KuzNetzov’s hand. All type specimens kept in the main collection have a red label with printed text “Ho- lotypus” or “Paratypus” and the name of the species written in ink by KuzNetzov’s hand. KuzNETzov never made genitalia slides and all genitalia preparations are mounted with sugar on the paper plates and put on the species needles under the locality labels. Surprisingly, types of several species described by Kuznetzov were not found in the main collection. However, three drawers of Vietnamese Tortricidae were found in the cabinet where KuzNetzov deposited all material he currently worked on. Some of those Tortricidae were determined by him and marked with the species name on a label. Others are undetermined or bear handwritten labels with the name of the genus or different comments (in Russian). All missing types were found in these drawers, but only a few of them were marked with red type labels. So specimens belong to the type series were discovered by comparison of their labels with the original descriptions. - Unless the user explicitly provides a URL or names a specific website to visit, always start at google.com. Open Google, type your search query, read the results, and follow links by clicking — do not jump directly to any URL, and do not construct or guess URLs from memory or training data.

- Apply any available filters: date range, category, author, language, file type, etc.

- Prefer specialized tools (ArXiv, Wikipedia, YouTube, direct download, etc.) when they directly match the task. Use browser automation only when no dedicated tool fits.
- Only Google Search is permitted as a search engine.
- For academic paper searches, prefer Google Scholar, arXiv, and DBLP.

Work carefully, efficiently, and stay within your assigned retrieval scope.

KuzNerzov from Vietnam are listed with short comments on the type series including descrip- tions of their labels. Colour images of the holotypes are given (col. pl. 7-9). Descriptions of 99 of five species are provided and their genitalia are figured. Zusammenfassung: 67 Arten die von V. Kuznetzov aus Vietnam beschrieben wurden, werden mit kurzen Kommentaren zur Ty- pusserie und deren Etikettierung versehen. Die Holotypen werden farbig abgebildet (col. pl. 7-9). Von fünf Arten werden die 99 beschrieben und deren Genitalien abgebildet. Introduction: VLADIMIR IvANovicH KuzNeEtzov (1929-2008) (figs 1-5) is one of the most famous modern Russian lepidopterologists. He was born 28.11.1929 in Kingisepp, Leningrad Region. His father was née Egorov and he was born into the family of a smith. Therefore he was known at school as a smith’s son, in Russian transcription as Kuznetzov (=Kuznetz’s son). Thus, the family name KUZNETZOV is in some sense a pseudonym. During The Second World War Kuznetzov lost his mother and lived in an orphanage until his father came back from the War. After that, VLADIMIR Kuznetzoy finished secondary school in Leningrad and entered the biological faculty of Leningrad State University in 1946. He finished there in 1951 and completed his PhD in 1954. In 1955 Kuz- NETZOV became a staff member at the Zoological Institute of the Russian Academy of Sciences in Leningrad, Russia (ZISP) where he worked for 52 years. He took part in several expeditions and published more than 200 papers devoted to Lepidoptera, especially Tortricidae. Most of his works dealt with the Palaearctic fauna, but some of them were based on material from the Oriental Regi- on. In total, KuzNEtzov described 394 taxa, 295 of them Tortricidae. He died 22. VIII 2008 in St. Petersburg and was cremated at Smolenskoe Cemetery. Twice in his lifetime, in 1986 and 1988, KuzNetzov visited Vietnam as a member of Soviet-Vietnamese zoological expeditions. The first field trip was carried out in spring and all material was collected in the Northern provinces: Son La, Vinh Phuc and Thai Nguyen (earlier Bac Thai). The second trip was in autumn (9.X1.-22.XII.) and during this time KuzNetzov visited the south of the country in the Gia Lai (earlier Gia Lai-Kon Tum) province. A huge amount of lepidopterous material was collected by KuzNETzov in Vietnam and all of it is now deposited in the collection of ZISP. As a result of his expeditionary work, Kuznetzov published 13 papers devoted to Tortricidae of Vietnam but only one of them was in English. In these works he listed 225 species, described 67 of them as new, and established 5 new genera. Investigation of the type material is an important part of all taxonomic studies but detailed descriptions of the species, with figured genitalia of both sexes and coloured images of the moths, make the work much easier. Descriptions of Tortricidae from Vietnam published by Kuznetzov in 1988-2003 are quite full and figures of genitalia structures are very good. Unfortunately, he gave no photos of the type specimens and all his descriptions were published in Russian. So the work with KUZNETzov’s papers is very com- plicated without knowledge of the Russian language. In recent years the volume of newly collected material from South-East Asia has really increased; a lot of new species are described recently from this region. At the same time, coloured images are very important for the comparison of new material with the species already described to avoid making synonyms. Since KuZNETzov’s types have never been examined by other workers, almost all of them are placed now in the same genera as in the original description. Very few of them were synonymized and mentioned by other workers at all. The reason is probably the difficulty in interpreting species described by Kuznetzov without images. Another problem is that some species were described by Kuznetzov based on a single specimen, in most cases g, and 99 are unknown. All Vietnamese Tortricidae collected by KuZNETZov were arranged taxonomically within the main collection of ZISP. Each speci- men has a standard white printed label with the name of the locality (in English). Most of them have a label with the name of the species written in ink by KuzNetzov’s hand. All type specimens kept in the main collection have a red label with printed text “Ho- lotypus” or “Paratypus” and the name of the species written in ink by KuzNetzov’s hand. KuzNETzov never made genitalia slides and all genitalia preparations are mounted with sugar on the paper plates and put on the species needles under the locality labels. Surprisingly, types of several species described by Kuznetzov were not found in the main collection. However, three drawers of Vietnamese Tortricidae were found in the cabinet where KuzNetzov deposited all material he currently worked on. Some of those Tortricidae were determined by him and marked with the species name on a label. Others are undetermined or bear handwritten labels with the name of the genus or different comments (in Russian). All missing types were found in these drawers, but only a few of them were marked with red type labels. So specimens belong to the type series were discovered by comparison of their labels with the original descriptions. Names of localities mentioned on KuzNEtzov’s labels often differ from modern names and in some cases it is difficult to find them on the map. ## Navigation policy

Loading large, unfiltered pages makes it hard to locate relevant information and risks exceeding LLM context length limits. Before loading any page, actively try to reduce its size:
- Use the site's search box with specific keywords rather than browsing index pages.
- Apply any available filters: date range, category, author, language, file type, etc.
- Prefer paginated or scoped views over full listing pages.

- Prefer specialized tools (ArXiv, Wikipedia, YouTube, direct download, etc.) when they directly match the task. Use browser automation only when no dedicated tool fits.
- Only Google Search is permitted as a search engine.
- For academic paper searches, prefer Google Scholar, arXiv, and DBLP.

Work carefully, efficiently, and stay within your assigned retrieval scope.

KUZNETZOv from Vietnam and deposited in the Zoological Institute, St. Petersburg by SVETLANA V. NEDOSHIVINA received 4.XTI.2009 Abstract: 67 species described by V. KuzNerzov from Vietnam are listed with short comments on the type series including descrip- tions of their labels. Colour images of the holotypes are given (col. pl. 7-9). Descriptions of 99 of five species are provided and their genitalia are figured. Zusammenfassung: 67 Arten die von V. Kuznetzov aus Vietnam beschrieben wurden, werden mit kurzen Kommentaren zur Ty- pusserie und deren Etikettierung versehen. Die Holotypen werden farbig abgebildet (col. pl. 7-9). Von fünf Arten werden die 99 beschrieben und deren Genitalien abgebildet. Introduction: VLADIMIR IvANovicH KuzNeEtzov (1929-2008) (figs 1-5) is one of the most famous modern Russian lepidopterologists. He was born 28.11.1929 in Kingisepp, Leningrad Region. His father was née Egorov and he was born into the family of a smith. Therefore he was known at school as a smith’s son, in Russian transcription as Kuznetzov (=Kuznetz’s son). Thus, the family name KUZNETZOV is in some sense a pseudonym. During The Second World War Kuznetzov lost his mother and lived in an orphanage until his father came back from the War. After that, VLADIMIR Kuznetzoy finished secondary school in Leningrad and entered the biological faculty of Leningrad State University in 1946. He finished there in 1951 and completed his PhD in 1954. In 1955 Kuz- NETZOV became a staff member at the Zoological Institute of the Russian Academy of Sciences in Leningrad, Russia (ZISP) where he worked for 52 years. He took part in several expeditions and published more than 200 papers devoted to Lepidoptera, especially Tortricidae. Most of his works dealt with the Palaearctic fauna, but some of them were based on material from the Oriental Regi- on. In total, KuzNEtzov described 394 taxa, 295 of them Tortricidae. He died 22. VIII 2008 in St. Petersburg and was cremated at Smolenskoe Cemetery. Twice in his lifetime, in 1986 and 1988, KuzNetzov visited Vietnam as a member of Soviet-Vietnamese zoological expeditions. The first field trip was carried out in spring and all material was collected in the Northern provinces: Son La, Vinh Phuc and Thai Nguyen (earlier Bac Thai). The second trip was in autumn (9.X1.-22.XII.) and during this time KuzNetzov visited the south of the country in the Gia Lai (earlier Gia Lai-Kon Tum) province. A huge amount of lepidopterous material was collected by KuzNETzov in Vietnam and all of it is now deposited in the collection of ZISP. As a result of his expeditionary work, Kuznetzov published 13 papers devoted to Tortricidae of Vietnam but only one of them was in English. In these works he listed 225 species, described 67 of them as new, and established 5 new genera. Investigation of the type material is an important part of all taxonomic studies but detailed descriptions of the species, with figured genitalia of both sexes and coloured images of the moths, make the work much easier. Descriptions of Tortricidae from Vietnam published by Kuznetzov in 1988-2003 are quite full and figures of genitalia structures are very good. Unfortunately, he gave no photos of the type specimens and all his descriptions were published in Russian. So the work with KUZNETzov’s papers is very com- plicated without knowledge of the Russian language. In recent years the volume of newly collected material from South-East Asia has really increased; a lot of new species are described recently from this region. At the same time, coloured images are very important for the comparison of new material with the species already described to avoid making synonyms. Since KuZNETzov’s types have never been examined by other workers, almost all of them are placed now in the same genera as in the original description. Very few of them were synonymized and mentioned by other workers at all. The reason is probably the difficulty in interpreting species described by Kuznetzov without images. Another problem is that some species were described by Kuznetzov based on a single specimen, in most cases g, and 99 are unknown. All Vietnamese Tortricidae collected by KuZNETZov were arranged taxonomically within the main collection of ZISP. Each speci- men has a standard white printed label with the name of the locality (in English). Most of them have a label with the name of the species written in ink by KuzNetzov’s hand. All type specimens kept in the main collection have a red label with printed text “Ho- lotypus” or “Paratypus” and the name of the species written in ink by KuzNetzov’s hand. KuzNETzov never made genitalia slides and all genitalia preparations are mounted with sugar on the paper plates and put on the species needles under the locality labels. Surprisingly, types of several species described by Kuznetzov were not found in the main collection. However, three drawers of Vietnamese Tortricidae were found in the cabinet where KuzNetzov deposited all material he currently worked on. Some of those Tortricidae were determined by him and marked with the species name on a label. Others are undetermined or bear handwritten labels with the name of the genus or different comments (in Russian). All missing types were found in these drawers, but only a few of them were marked with red type labels. So specimens belong to the type series were discovered by comparison of their labels with the original descriptions. Names of localities mentioned on KuzNEtzov’s labels often differ from modern names and in some cases it is difficult to find them on the map. Therefore the list of collecting localities by Kuznetzov is given below with notes on real names and coordinates of corresponding places. 1. Prov. Sonla, Naniu - According to the map published by Kuznerzov in 2000, this locality is situated between 22° 07° and 22° 11° N, 102° 59° and 103° 09° E. KUZNETZOv from Vietnam and deposited in the Zoological Institute, St. Petersburg by SVETLANA V. NEDOSHIVINA received 4.XTI.2009 Abstract: 67 species described by V. KuzNerzov from Vietnam are listed with short comments on the type series including descrip- tions of their labels. Colour images of the holotypes are given (col. pl. 7-9). Descriptions of 99 of five species are provided and their genitalia are figured. Zusammenfassung: 67 Arten die von V. Kuznetzov aus Vietnam beschrieben wurden, werden mit kurzen Kommentaren zur Ty- pusserie und deren Etikettierung versehen. Die Holotypen werden farbig abgebildet (col. pl. 7-9). Von fünf Arten werden die 99 beschrieben und deren Genitalien abgebildet. Introduction: VLADIMIR IvANovicH KuzNeEtzov (1929-2008) (figs 1-5) is one of the most famous modern Russian lepidopterologists. He was born 28.11.1929 in Kingisepp, Leningrad Region. His father was née Egorov and he was born into the family of a smith. Therefore he was known at school as a smith’s son, in Russian transcription as Kuznetzov (=Kuznetz’s son). Thus, the family name KUZNETZOV is in some sense a pseudonym. During The Second World War Kuznetzov lost his mother and lived in an orphanage until his father came back from the War. After that, VLADIMIR Kuznetzoy finished secondary school in Leningrad and entered the biological faculty of Leningrad State University in 1946. He finished there in 1951 and completed his PhD in 1954. In 1955 Kuz- NETZOV became a staff member at the Zoological Institute of the Russian Academy of Sciences in Leningrad, Russia (ZISP) where he worked for 52 years. He took part in several expeditions and published more than 200 papers devoted to Lepidoptera, especially Tortricidae. Most of his works dealt with the Palaearctic fauna, but some of them were based on material from the Oriental Regi- on. In total, KuzNEtzov described 394 taxa, 295 of them Tortricidae. He died 22. VIII 2008 in St. Petersburg and was cremated at Smolenskoe Cemetery. Twice in his lifetime, in 1986 and 1988, KuzNetzov visited Vietnam as a member of Soviet-Vietnamese zoological expeditions. The first field trip was carried out in spring and all material was collected in the Northern provinces: Son La, Vinh Phuc and Thai Nguyen (earlier Bac Thai). The second trip was in autumn (9.X1.-22.XII.) and during this time KuzNetzov visited the south of the country in the Gia Lai (earlier Gia Lai-Kon Tum) province. A huge amount of lepidopterous material was collected by KuzNETzov in Vietnam and all of it is now deposited in the collection of ZISP. As a result of his expeditionary work, Kuznetzov published 13 papers devoted to Tortricidae of Vietnam but only one of them was in English. In these works he listed 225 species, described 67 of them as new, and established 5 new genera. Investigation of the type material is an important part of all taxonomic studies but detailed descriptions of the species, with figured genitalia of both sexes and coloured images of the moths, make the work much easier. Descriptions of Tortricidae from Vietnam published by Kuznetzov in 1988-2003 are quite full and figures of genitalia structures are very good. Unfortunately, he gave no photos of the type specimens and all his descriptions were published in Russian. So the work with KUZNETzov’s papers is very com- plicated without knowledge of the Russian language. In recent years the volume of newly collected material from South-East Asia has really increased; a lot of new species are described recently from this region. At the same time, coloured images are very important for the comparison of new material with the species already described to avoid making synonyms. Since KuZNETzov’s types have never been examined by other workers, almost all of them are placed now in the same genera as in the original description. Very few of them were synonymized and mentioned by other workers at all. The reason is probably the difficulty in interpreting species described by Kuznetzov without images. Another problem is that some species were described by Kuznetzov based on a single specimen, in most cases g, and 99 are unknown. All Vietnamese Tortricidae collected by KuZNETZov were arranged taxonomically within the main collection of ZISP. Each speci- men has a standard white printed label with the name of the locality (in English). Most of them have a label with the name of the species written in ink by KuzNetzov’s hand. All type specimens kept in the main collection have a red label with printed text “Ho- lotypus” or “Paratypus” and the name of the species written in ink by KuzNetzov’s hand. KuzNETzov never made genitalia slides and all genitalia preparations are mounted with sugar on the paper plates and put on the species needles under the locality labels. Surprisingly, types of several species described by Kuznetzov were not found in the main collection. However, three drawers of Vietnamese Tortricidae were found in the cabinet where KuzNetzov deposited all material he currently worked on. Some of those Tortricidae were determined by him and marked with the species name on a label. Others are undetermined or bear handwritten labels with the name of the genus or different comments (in Russian). All missing types were found in these drawers, but only a few of them were marked with red type labels. So specimens belong to the type series were discovered by comparison of their labels with the original descriptions. Names of localities mentioned on KuzNEtzov’s labels often differ from modern names and in some cases it is difficult to find them on the map. Therefore the list of collecting localities by Kuznetzov is given below with notes on real names and coordinates of corresponding places. 1. Prov. Sonla, Naniu - According to the map published by Kuznerzov in 2000, this locality is situated between 22° 07° and 22° 11° N, 102° 59° and 103° 09° E. Introduction: VLADIMIR IvANovicH KuzNeEtzov (1929-2008) (figs 1-5) is one of the most famous modern Russian lepidopterologists. 
He was born 28.11.1929 in Kingisepp, Leningrad Region. His father was née Egorov and he was born into the family of a smith. 
Therefore he was known at school as a smith’s son, in Russian transcription as Kuznetzov (=Kuznetz’s son). Thus, the family name 
KUZNETZOV is in some sense a pseudonym. During The Second World War Kuznetzov lost his mother and lived in an orphanage 
until his father came back from the War. After that, VLADIMIR Kuznetzoy finished secondary school in Leningrad and entered the 
biological faculty of Leningrad State University in 1946. He finished there in 1951 and completed his PhD in 1954. In 1955 Kuz- 
NETZOV became a staff member at the Zoological Institute of the Russian Academy of Sciences in Leningrad, Russia (ZISP) where 
he worked for 52 years. He took part in several expeditions and published more than 200 papers devoted to Lepidoptera, especially 
Tortricidae. Most of his works dealt with the Palaearctic fauna, but some of them were based on material from the Oriental Regi- 
on. In total, KuzNEtzov described 394 taxa, 295 of them Tortricidae. He died 22. VIII 2008 in St. Petersburg and was cremated at 
Smolenskoe Cemetery. 


Twice in his lifetime, in 1986 and 1988, KuzNetzov visited Vietnam as a member of Soviet-Vietnamese zoological expeditions. 
The first field trip was carried out in spring and all material was collected in the Northern provinces: Son La, Vinh Phuc and Thai 
Nguyen (earlier Bac Thai). The second trip was in autumn (9.X1.-22.XII.) and during this time KuzNetzov visited the south of the 
country in the Gia Lai (earlier Gia Lai-Kon Tum) province. A huge amount of lepidopterous material was collected by KuzNETzov 
in Vietnam and all of it is now deposited in the collection of ZISP. As a result of his expeditionary work, Kuznetzov published 13 
papers devoted to Tortricidae of Vietnam but only one of them was in English. In these works he listed 225 species, described 67 of 
them as new, and established 5 new genera. 


Investigation of the type material is an important part of all taxonomic studies but detailed descriptions of the species, with figured 
genitalia of both sexes and coloured images of the moths, make the work much easier. Descriptions of Tortricidae from Vietnam 
published by Kuznetzov in 1988-2003 are quite full and figures of genitalia structures are very good. Unfortunately, he gave no 
photos of the type specimens and all his descriptions were published in Russian. So the work with KUZNETzov’s papers is very com- 
plicated without knowledge of the Russian language. 


In recent years the volume of newly collected material from South-East Asia has really increased; a lot of new species are described 
recently from this region. At the same time, coloured images are very important for the comparison of new material with the species 
already described to avoid making synonyms. Since KuZNETzov’s types have never been examined by other workers, almost all of them 
are placed now in the same genera as in the original description. Very few of them were synonymized and mentioned by other workers 
at all. The reason is probably the difficulty in interpreting species described by Kuznetzov without images. Another problem is that 
some species were described by Kuznetzov based on a single specimen, in most cases g, and 99 are unknown. 


All Vietnamese Tortricidae collected by KuZNETZov were arranged taxonomically within the main collection of ZISP. Each speci- 
men has a standard white printed label with the name of the locality (in English). Most of them have a label with the name of the 
species written in ink by KuzNetzov’s hand. All type specimens kept in the main collection have a red label with printed text “Ho- 
lotypus” or “Paratypus” and the name of the species written in ink by KuzNetzov’s hand. KuzNETzov never made genitalia slides 
and all genitalia preparations are mounted with sugar on the paper plates and put on the species needles under the locality labels. 
Surprisingly, types of several species described by Kuznetzov were not found in the main collection. However, three drawers of 
Vietnamese Tortricidae were found in the cabinet where KuzNetzov deposited all material he currently worked on. Some of those 
Tortricidae were determined by him and marked with the species name on a label. Others are undetermined or bear handwritten

the original descriptions. Names of localities mentioned on KuzNEtzov’s labels often differ from modern names and in some cases it

KUZNETZOv from Vietnam and deposited in the Zoological Institute, St. Petersburg by SVETLANA V. NEDOSHIVINA received 4.XTI.2009 Abstract: 67 species described by V. KuzNerzov from Vietnam are listed with short comments on the type series including descrip- tions of their labels. Colour images of the holotypes are given (col. pl. 7-9). Descriptions of 99 of five species are provided and their genitalia are figured. Zusammenfassung: 67 Arten die von V. Kuznetzov aus Vietnam beschrieben wurden, werden mit kurzen Kommentaren zur Ty- pusserie und deren Etikettierung versehen. Die Holotypen werden farbig abgebildet (col. pl. 7-9). Von fünf Arten werden die 99 beschrieben und deren Genitalien abgebildet. Introduction: VLADIMIR IvANovicH KuzNeEtzov (1929-2008) (figs 1-5) is one of the most famous modern Russian lepidopterologists. He was born 28.11.1929 in Kingisepp, Leningrad Region. His father was née Egorov and he was born into the family of a smith. Therefore he was known at school as a smith’s son, in Russian transcription as Kuznetzov (=Kuznetz’s son). Thus, the family name KUZNETZOV is in some sense a pseudonym. During The Second World War Kuznetzov lost his mother and lived in an orphanage until his father came back from the War. After that, VLADIMIR Kuznetzoy finished secondary school in Leningrad and entered the biological faculty of Leningrad State University in 1946. He finished there in 1951 and completed his PhD in 1954. In 1955 Kuz- NETZOV became a staff member at the Zoological Institute of the Russian Academy of Sciences in Leningrad, Russia (ZISP) where he worked for 52 years. He took part in several expeditions and published more than 200 papers devoted to Lepidoptera, especially Tortricidae. Most of his works dealt with the Palaearctic fauna, but some of them were based on material from the Oriental Regi- on. In total, KuzNEtzov described 394 taxa, 295 of them Tortricidae. He died 22. VIII 2008 in St. Petersburg and was cremated at Smolenskoe Cemetery. Twice in his lifetime, in 1986 and 1988, KuzNetzov visited Vietnam as a member of Soviet-Vietnamese zoological expeditions. The first field trip was carried out in spring and all material was collected in the Northern provinces: Son La, Vinh Phuc and Thai Nguyen (earlier Bac Thai). The second trip was in autumn (9.X1.-22.XII.) and during this time KuzNetzov visited the south of the country in the Gia Lai (earlier Gia Lai-Kon Tum) province. A huge amount of lepidopterous material was collected by KuzNETzov in Vietnam and all of it is now deposited in the collection of ZISP. As a result of his expeditionary work, Kuznetzov published 13 papers devoted to Tortricidae of Vietnam but only one of them was in English. In these works he listed 225 species, described 67 of them as new, and established 5 new genera. Investigation of the type material is an important part of all taxonomic studies but detailed descriptions of the species, with figured genitalia of both sexes and coloured images of the moths, make the work much easier. Descriptions of Tortricidae from Vietnam published by Kuznetzov in 1988-2003 are quite full and figures of genitalia structures are very good. Unfortunately, he gave no photos of the type specimens and all his descriptions were published in Russian. So the work with KUZNETzov’s papers is very com- plicated without knowledge of the Russian language. In recent years the volume of newly collected material from South-East Asia has really increased; a lot of new species are described recently from this region. At the same time, coloured images are very important for the comparison of new material with the species already described to avoid making synonyms. Since KuZNETzov’s types have never been examined by other workers, almost all of them are placed now in the same genera as in the original description. Very few of them were synonymized and mentioned by other workers at all. The reason is probably the difficulty in interpreting species described by Kuznetzov without images. Another problem is that some species were described by Kuznetzov based on a single specimen, in most cases g, and 99 are unknown. All Vietnamese Tortricidae collected by KuZNETZov were arranged taxonomically within the main collection of ZISP. Each speci- men has a standard white printed label with the name of the locality (in English). Most of them have a label with the name of the species written in ink by KuzNetzov’s hand. All type specimens kept in the main collection have a red label with printed text “Ho- lotypus” or “Paratypus” and the name of the species written in ink by KuzNetzov’s hand. KuzNETzov never made genitalia slides and all genitalia preparations are mounted with sugar on the paper plates and put on the species needles under the locality labels. Surprisingly, types of several species described by Kuznetzov were not found in the main collection. However, three drawers of Vietnamese Tortricidae were found in the cabinet where KuzNetzov deposited all material he currently worked on. Some of those Tortricidae were determined by him and marked with the species name on a label. Others are undetermined or bear handwritten labels with the name of the genus or different comments (in Russian). All missing types were found in these drawers, but only a few of them were marked with red type labels. So specimens belong to the type series were discovered by comparison of their labels with the original descriptions. Names of localities mentioned on KuzNEtzov’s labels often differ from modern names and in some cases it is difficult to find them on the map. Therefore the list of collecting localities by Kuznetzov is given below with notes on real names and coordinates of corresponding places. 1. Prov. by 
SVETLANA V. NEDOSHIVINA 
received 4.XTI.2009 


Abstract: 67 species described by V. KuzNerzov from Vietnam are listed with short comments on the type series including descrip- 
tions of their labels. Colour images of the holotypes are given (col. pl. 7-9). Descriptions of 99 of five species are provided and their 
genitalia are figured. 


Zusammenfassung: 67 Arten die von V. Kuznetzov aus Vietnam beschrieben wurden, werden mit kurzen Kommentaren zur Ty- 
pusserie und deren Etikettierung versehen. Die Holotypen werden farbig abgebildet (col. pl. 7-9). Von fünf Arten werden die 99 
beschrieben und deren Genitalien abgebildet. 


Introduction: VLADIMIR IvANovicH KuzNeEtzov (1929-2008) (figs 1-5) is one of the most famous modern Russian lepidopterologists. 
He was born 28.11.1929 in Kingisepp, Leningrad Region. His father was née Egorov and he was born into the family of a smith. 
Therefore he was known at school as a smith’s son, in Russian transcription as Kuznetzov (=Kuznetz’s son). Thus, the family name 
KUZNETZOV is in some sense a pseudonym. During The Second World War Kuznetzov lost his mother and lived in an orphanage 
until his father came back from the War. After that, VLADIMIR Kuznetzoy finished secondary school in Leningrad and entered the 
biological faculty of Leningrad State University in 1946. He finished there in 1951 and completed his PhD in 1954. In 1955 Kuz- 
NETZOV became a staff member at the Zoological Institute of the Russian Academy of Sciences in Leningrad, Russia (ZISP) where 
he worked for 52 years. He took part in several expeditions and published more than 200 papers devoted to Lepidoptera, especially 
Tortricidae. Most of his works dealt with the Palaearctic fauna, but some of them were based on material from the Oriental Regi- 
on. In total, KuzNEtzov described 394 taxa, 295 of them Tortricidae. He died 22. VIII 2008 in St. Petersburg and was cremated at 
Smolenskoe Cemetery. 


Twice in his lifetime, in 1986 and 1988, KuzNetzov visited Vietnam as a member of Soviet-Vietnamese zoological expeditions. 
The first field trip was carried out in spring and all material was collected in the Northern provinces: Son La, Vinh Phuc and Thai 
Nguyen (earlier Bac Thai). The second trip was in autumn (9.X1.-22.XII.) and during this time KuzNetzov visited the south of the 
country in the Gia Lai (earlier Gia Lai-Kon Tum) province. A huge amount of lepidopterous material was collected by KuzNETzov 
in Vietnam and all of it is now deposited in the collection of ZISP. As a result of his expeditionary work, Kuznetzov published 13 
papers devoted to Tortricidae of Vietnam but only one of them was in English. In these works he listed 225 species, described 67 of 
them as new, and established 5 new genera. 


Investigation of the type material is an important part of all taxonomic studies but detailed descriptions of the species, with figured 
genitalia of both sexes and coloured images of the moths, make the work much easier. Descriptions of Tortricidae from Vietnam 
published by Kuznetzov in 1988-2003 are quite full and figures of genitalia structures are very good. Unfortunately, he gave no 
photos of the type specimens and all his descriptions were published in Russian. So the work with KUZNETzov’s papers is very com- 
plicated without knowledge of the Russian language. 


In recent years the volume of newly collected material from South-East Asia has really increased; a lot of new species are described 
recently from this region. At the same time, coloured images are very important for the comparison of new material with the species 
already described to avoid making synonyms. Since KuZNETzov’s types have never been examined by other workers, almost all of them 
are placed now in the same genera as in the original description. Very few of them were synonymized and mentioned by other workers 
at all. The reason is probably the difficulty in interpreting species described by Kuznetzov without images. Another problem is that 
some species were described by Kuznetzov based on a single specimen, in most cases g, and 99 are unknown. 


All Vietnamese Tortricidae collected by KuZNETZov were arranged taxonomically within the main collection of ZISP. Each speci- 
men has a standard white printed label with the name of the locality (in English). Most of them have a label with the name of the 
species written in ink by KuzNetzov’s hand. All type specimens kept in the main collection have a red label with printed text “Ho- 
lotypus” or “Paratypus” and the name of the species written in ink by KuzNetzov’s hand. KuzNETzov never made genitalia slides 
and all genitalia preparations are mounted with sugar on the paper plates and put on the species needles under the locality labels. 
Surprisingly, types of several species described by Kuznetzov were not found in the main collection. However, three drawers of 
Vietnamese Tortricidae were found in the cabinet where KuzNetzov deposited all material he currently worked on. Some of those 
Tortricidae were determined by him and marked with the species name on a label. Others are undetermined or bear handwritten 
labels with the name of the genus or different comments (in Russian). All missing types were found in these drawers, but only a few 
of them were marked with red type labels. So specimens belong to the type series were discovered by comparison of their labels with 
the original descriptions. Names of localities mentioned on KuzNEtzov’s labels often differ from modern names and in some cases it 
is difficult to find them on the map. Therefore the list of collecting localities by Kuznetzov is given below with notes on real names 
and coordinates of corresponding places. 
1. Prov. Sonla, Naniu - According to the map published by Kuznerzov in 2000, this locality is situated between 22° 07° and 22° 
11° N, 102° 59° and 103° 09° E. Probably this point on the map was identified by KuzNetzov inexactly and actually corres- 
ponds to Ban Nam Nhié situated at 22° 08‘ N, 102° 45‘ E. 
2. Prov. Sonla, Chiengkhouan or Chienghouan - Province Son La, Ban Chiéng Khoang, 21° 33° N, 103° 40° E.

Title: A catalogue of type specimens of the Tortricidae described by V. I. Kuznetzov from Vietnam and deposited in the Zoological Institute, St. Petersburg
Author: Svetlana V. Nedoshivina
Publication: Atalanta 41 (3/4): 335‑347, Würzburg (2010)
Received: 4.XII.2009
Full-text source: Internet Archive (PDF and plain-text versions available)

Relevant Sections on Specimen Deposition:

1. Abstract – Purpose and Scope
“Abstract: 67 species described by V. Kuznetzov from Vietnam are listed with short comments on the type series including descriptions of their labels. Colour images of the holotypes are given (col. pl. 7‑9). Descriptions of 99 of five species are provided and their genitalia are figured.”

Key point: The catalogue explicitly lists all type specimens of Kuznetzov’s Vietnamese Tortricidae and provides data on their labels and deposition.

2. Introduction – Collection Location and Labeling
“All Vietnamese Tortricidae collected by Kuznetzov were arranged taxonomically within the main collection of ZISP (Zoological Institute of the Russian Academy of Sciences, St. Petersburg). Each specimen has a standard white printed label with the name of the locality (in English). Most of them have a label with the name of the species written in ink by Kuznetzov’s hand. All type specimens kept in the main collection have a red label with printed text ‘Holotypus’ or ‘Paratypus’ and the name of the species written in ink by Kuznetzov’s hand.”

“Kuznetzov never made genitalia slides and all genitalia preparations are mounted with sugar on paper plates and put on the species needles under the locality labels.”

“Surprisingly, types of several species described by Kuznetzov were not found in the main collection. However, three drawers of Vietnamese Tortricidae were found in the cabinet where Kuznetzov deposited all material he currently worked on. Some of those Tortricidae were determined by him and marked with the species name on a label. Others are undetermined or bear handwritten labels with the name of the genus or different comments (in Russian). All missing types were found in these drawers, but only a few of them were marked with red type labels. So specimens belonging to the type series were discovered by comparison of their labels with the original descriptions.”

Key points:
- All Kuznetzov’s Vietnamese material is housed in the Zoological Institute, St. Petersburg (ZISP).
- Type specimens are distinguished by red printed labels (“Holotypus”/“Paratypus”) with handwritten species names.
- Specimens not originally found in the main collection were located in three dedicated drawers where Kuznetzov kept his working material.

3. Structure of the Catalogue – How Deposition Information Is Presented
For each of the 67 species, the catalogue provides:

1. Original reference (publication details).
2. Types: Number of specimens in the type series according to the original description, plus their label data.
3. Comments: Additional data on the type series and the number of type specimens actually deposited in the collection of ZISP. This includes notes on missing paratypes, condition of holotypes, and whether specimens were found in the main collection or in the working drawers.
4. Distribution based on published records and material held in ZISP.

4. Example Entry (Species #1 – abstrusana)
“1. abstrusana Kuznetzov, 1988 (colour plate 8: 36)
Temnolopha abstrusana Kuznetzov, 1988, Trudy vsesoyuznogo entomologicheskogo obshchestva 70: 172, fig. 5: 2.
Types: Holotype ♂, N. Vietnam, Hanoi, 2.IV.1986, V. Kuznetzov leg. – Paratype: 1 ♂, N. Vietnam, prov. Vinhphu, Tamdao, 11.IV.1986, V. Kuznetzov leg.
Comments: The ♀ of this species is still unknown.
Distribution: North Vietnam: Hanoi, Tam Dao.”

Note: The “Types” section records the original type series; the “Comments” section adds any discrepancies between the described series and the specimens actually present in ZISP.

5. Taxonomic Appendix – Descriptions of Previously Unknown Females
The paper includes descriptions of the females of five species whose females were unknown until 2010:
- Statherotis diakonoffi Kuznetzov, 1988
- Dicnecidia fumidana Kuznetzov, 1997
- Cimeliomorpha nabokovi Kuznetzov, 1997
- Neocalyptis sodaliana Kuznetzov, 1992
- Homona superbana Kuznetzov, 1992

Each description is accompanied by genitalia illustrations and references to the deposited material (with slide numbers, e.g., GS. SVN09058).

Summary of Deposition Information:
Repository: Zoological Institute of the Russian Academy of Sciences, St. Petersburg (ZISP)
Collection status: – Main collection (taxonomically arranged) – Three additional drawers of working material
Labeling: – Standard white printed locality labels (English) – Handwritten species labels (Kuznetzov’s ink) – Red printed “Holotypus”/“Paratypus” labels for types
Genitalia preparations: Mounted with sugar on paper plates, placed on species needles under locality labels
Catalogue coverage: 67 species described by Kuznetzov from Vietnam; each entry includes type-series data and notes on actual specimens present in ZISP
Missing/lost types: Noted where specimens are absent from the main collection; some were later found in the working drawers

Access to the Full Paper:

– Download options: PDF, EPUB, plain text (DjVu), etc.
- Direct link to full text: https://archive.org/stream/atalanta-41-335-347/atalanta-41-335-347_djvu.txt (plain-text version used for this extraction)

The 2010 catalogue by Nedoshivina fulfills the user’s request by providing detailed information on the deposition of Kuznetzov’s Vietnamese Tortricidae type specimens. It confirms that all material is housed in the Zoological Institute, St. Petersburg (ZISP), describes the labeling system, records discrepancies between originally described type series and the actual specimens present, and includes notes on specimens found in Kuznetzov’s working drawers. The paper is an essential reference for anyone studying these taxa or needing to locate the physical type specimens.

messages.content:
You are the WebSurfer agent. You retrieve information from the web by navigating and interacting with pages, exactly as a human would.

## Navigation policy
- Unless the user explicitly provides a URL or names a specific website to visit, always start at google.com. Open Google, type your search query, read the results, and follow links by clicking — do not jump directly to any URL, and do not construct or guess URLs from memory or training data.

## Page size management (critical)
Loading large, unfiltered pages makes it hard to locate relevant information and risks exceeding LLM context length limits. Before loading any page, actively try to reduce its size:
- Use the site's search box with specific keywords rather than browsing index pages.
- Apply any available filters: date range, category, author, language, file type, etc.
- Prefer paginated or scoped views over full listing pages.

## Tool selection
- Prefer specialized tools (ArXiv, Wikipedia, YouTube, direct download, etc.) when they directly match the task. Use browser automation only when no dedicated tool fits.
- Only Google Search is permitted as a search engine.
- For academic paper searches, prefer Google Scholar, arXiv, and DBLP.

## Output
- Produce well-structured, detailed output as required. Extract only what is relevant to the task.
- If you use browser tools to save any content, the browser will store it under the directory: [<PROJECT_ROOT>/tmp/browser_wp]. This is enforced by the browser itself — you only need to report the file path in your output when needed.

Work carefully, efficiently, and stay within your assigned retrieval scope.

## Navigation policy
- Unless the user explicitly provides a URL or names a specific website to visit, always start at google.com. Open Google, type your search query, read the results, and follow links by clicking — do not jump directly to any URL, and do not construct or guess URLs from memory or training data.

## Page size management (critical)
Loading large, unfiltered pages makes it hard to locate relevant information and risks exceeding LLM context length limits. Before loading any page, actively try to reduce its size:

- Apply any available filters: date range, category, author, language, file type, etc.
- Prefer paginated or scoped views over full listing pages.

- Prefer specialized tools (ArXiv, Wikipedia, YouTube, direct download, etc.) when they directly match the task. Use browser automation only when no dedicated tool fits.
- Only Google Search is permitted as a search engine.
- For academic paper searches, prefer Google Scholar, arXiv, and DBLP.

Work carefully, efficiently, and stay within your assigned retrieval scope.

messages.content:
You are the WebSurfer agent. You retrieve information from the web by navigating and interacting with pages, exactly as a human would.

## Navigation policy
- Unless the user explicitly provides a URL or names a specific website to visit, always start at google.com. Open Google, type your search query, read the results, and follow links by clicking — do not jump directly to any URL, and do not construct or guess URLs from memory or training data.

## Page size management (critical)
Loading large, unfiltered pages makes it hard to locate relevant information and risks exceeding LLM context length limits. Before loading any page, actively try to reduce its size:
- Use the site's search box with specific keywords rather than browsing index pages.
- Apply any available filters: date range, category, author, language, file type, etc.
- Prefer paginated or scoped views over full listing pages.

## Tool selection
- Prefer specialized tools (ArXiv, Wikipedia, YouTube, direct download, etc.) when they directly match the task. Use browser automation only when no dedicated tool fits.
- Only Google Search is permitted as a search engine.
- For academic paper searches, prefer Google Scholar, arXiv, and DBLP.

You are the WebSurfer agent. You retrieve information from the web by navigating and interacting with pages, exactly as a human would.

## Navigation policy
- Unless the user explicitly provides a URL or names a specific website to visit, always start at google.com. Open Google, type your search query, read the results, and follow links by clicking — do not jump directly to any URL, and do not construct or guess URLs from memory or training data.

## Page size management (critical)
Loading large, unfiltered pages makes it hard to locate relevant information and risks exceeding LLM context length limits. Before loading any page, actively try to reduce its size:
- Use the site's search box with specific keywords rather than browsing index pages.
- Apply any available filters: date range, category, author, language, file type, etc.
- Prefer paginated or scoped views over full listing pages.

## Tool selection
- Prefer specialized tools (ArXiv, Wikipedia, YouTube, direct download, etc.) when they directly match the task. Use browser automation only when no dedicated tool fits.
- Only Google Search is permitted as a search engine.
- For academic paper searches, prefer Google Scholar, arXiv, and DBLP.

## Output
- Produce well-structured, detailed output as required. Extract only what is relevant to the task.
- If you use browser tools to save any content, the browser will store it under the directory: [<PROJECT_ROOT>/tmp/browser_wp]. This is enforced by the browser itself — you only need to report the file path in your output when needed.

Work carefully, efficiently, and stay within your assigned retrieval scope.

You are the WebSurfer agent. You retrieve information from the web by navigating and interacting with pages, exactly as a human would.

## Navigation policy
- Unless the user explicitly provides a URL or names a specific website to visit, always start at google.com. Open Google, type your search query, read the results, and follow links by clicking — do not jump directly to any URL, and do not construct or guess URLs from memory or training data.

## Page size management (critical)
Loading large, unfiltered pages makes it hard to locate relevant information and risks exceeding LLM context length limits. Before loading any page, actively try to reduce its size:
- Use the site's search box with specific keywords rather than browsing index pages.
- Apply any available filters: date range, category, author, language, file type, etc.
- Prefer paginated or scoped views over full listing pages.

## Tool selection
- Prefer specialized tools (ArXiv, Wikipedia, YouTube, direct download, etc.) when they directly match the task. Use browser automation only when no dedicated tool fits.
- Only Google Search is permitted as a search engine.
- For academic paper searches, prefer Google Scholar, arXiv, and DBLP.

## Output
- Produce well-structured, detailed output as required. Extract only what is relevant to the task.
- If you use browser tools to save any content, the browser will store it under the directory: [<PROJECT_ROOT>/tmp/browser_wp]. This is enforced by the browser itself — you only need to report the file path in your output when needed.

Work carefully, efficiently, and stay within your assigned retrieval scope.

You are the WebSurfer agent. You retrieve information from the web by navigating and interacting with pages, exactly as a human would.

## Navigation policy
- Unless the user explicitly provides a URL or names a specific website to visit, always start at google.com. Open Google, type your search query, read the results, and follow links by clicking — do not jump directly to any URL, and do not construct or guess URLs from memory or training data.

## Page size management (critical)
Loading large, unfiltered pages makes it hard to locate relevant information and risks exceeding LLM context length limits. Before loading any page, actively try to reduce its size:
- Use the site's search box with specific keywords rather than browsing index pages.
- Apply any available filters: date range, category, author, language, file type, etc.
- Prefer paginated or scoped views over full listing pages.

## Tool selection
- Prefer specialized tools (ArXiv, Wikipedia, YouTube, direct download, etc.) when they directly match the task. Use browser automation only when no dedicated tool fits.
- Only Google Search is permitted as a search engine.
- For academic paper searches, prefer Google Scholar, arXiv, and DBLP.

## Output
- Produce well-structured, detailed output as required. Extract only what is relevant to the task.
- If you use browser tools to save any content, the browser will store it under the directory: [<PROJECT_ROOT>/tmp/browser_wp]. This is enforced by the browser itself — you only need to report the file path in your output when needed.

Work carefully, efficiently, and stay within your assigned retrieval scope.
